The live server speaks Model Context Protocol: an AI agent can connect to /mcp and read a running session's snapshot, a courtier's character sheet, or its command log as typed tools.
A city's district count is seeded from its EU4 1444 development — administration, trade, and manpower summed — while an ordinary province gets a single village centre on its one urban plot.

A band that stops to settle founds a foraging camp led by a captain: its people work the land and build a hunting camp on their plot, and only once the food surplus piles up does the camp grow into a village — booting a ruler, banks and markets — or, on poor ground, strike camp and move on.

Zoom deep into any city and its plots bloom into Civ6 district hexes — a star for the centre, a flask for a campus, a coin for the market — while the buildings a colony has actually researched ring the town.
The Serpentspine underworld is a whole second map plane of 385 sunless provinces, where a fixed 14-hour lamplit shift makes dwarven toil out-produce a full surface day.
There is no sun underground, so cavern colonies farm cave-fungus grown on the bare rock floor: meager food, but the ore-rich stone repays the miners.
The tiger-folk Harimari of Anbennar mature fast: their children enter the workforce at age nine, where a human child must wait until fifteen.
Only human names are hand-authored into CivStudio; every other race's names are generated on demand from Anbennar's own culture files and cached.
The calendar is pre-Reformation: Sunday is the only weekly rest day, Saturday is a workday, and 31 fixed feasts outrank even a Sunday.
On a feast day every commoner firm shuts and only the nobles labor, because the strategic export sector works straight through the holy days.
People age and die on Coale-Demeny West Level 3 life tables, a real historical mortality schedule whose life expectancy at birth is just twenty-five years.
Every person carries twelve RimWorld-style skills with passions; a skill you are passionate about never fades, while unused mastery slowly rusts back toward competence.
Daylight literally scales your labor output, computed by a vendored sunrise-sunset calculator; near London's midsummer the astronomical twilight can last the entire night.
Dead laborers are not inherited: the ruler feeds a pool of peasants and promotes the ablest to fill each empty household, making replacement meritocratic rather than hereditary.
Ruler colonies are designed to collapse: the labor model only replaces the dead one-for-one, so every settlement eventually winds down as its reserve drains.
There are no founding nobles at all; the entire aristocracy is raised from the ablest laborers, re-banked from copper into silver upon their elevation.
Wealth climbs a currency ladder: commoners bank in copper, nobles in silver, rulers in gold, and money-changers skim a fee at every exchange.
Caravans march like a Roman army, and a band so long that it spends the whole day filing out of camp makes zero net progress.
A wandering band forages food and mines ore as it marches, yet a medieval caravan literally cannot see an oil or uranium deposit it lacks the tech to know.
The tech tree is 338 nodes lifted from Caveman2Cosmos, the Prehistoric-to-Renaissance slice carved out of that mod's sprawling 943-technology graph.
The world is the whole imported Anbennar map: 5,264 provinces nested inside 1,375 areas, 153 regions and 29 super-regions.
Same seed, same story: economy, naming, mortality, skills and terrain each ride their own salted random stream so no draw ever disturbs another.
Rivers are read straight from Anbennar's river bitmap, which encodes water width by color and even marks each source, confluence and split.

Every river is traced backwards from the sea: each cell touching open water is a mouth, and the water's path is the way home to one. That is also how a river knows its width — count everything draining through it, and it doubles its catchment to widen a step.
Anbennar's magical trade goods get their own class, where damestear, mithril, precursor relics and serpentbloom stand apart from mere grain and iron.
Explore through nine continuous zoom bands, from a 1x EU4-style strategy atlas all the way down to a 256x city-builder view of building lots.
Some forests are stranger than others: crimson blood-magic bloodgroves, teal fey gladeways and pale glaciers each get their own terrain, art and yields.
Your privy council is staffed by real nobles from the leader's court — the ablest scholar heads Technology, and when one dies a successor quietly takes the seat.
Every advisor wears their own race's Anbennar portrait; a tiger-folk Harimari councillor really does look like a tiger in a silk robe.
Over 1,270 Caveman2Cosmos buildings are woven into the tech tree — each node reveals what it unlocks as a grid of real building icons, dimmed until your colony has researched its way there.
The Technology advisor is a full-canvas map-mode: every tech shows a coloured spectrum bar of the buildings it grants, and clicking one opens its Civilopedia entry in the rail.

When an explorer expedition marches home, its foraged haul is sold on the enjoyment market, the crown takes a tax, the ablest returnee is ennobled, and the rest found their own banked households — a landless peasant can come home a lord.
Landed households farm their own home plot for food that drops straight into the larder, never touching the market — so when prices spiral, the people who hold land still eat.

Zoom in and hover a plot — its name is a real place on Earth. Every region of the world is mapped to a country and each plot borrows the nearest real town or landmark from it, in the original script, so the dwarven Serpentspine reads like the Alps and Rahen like India.

The band chip in the top bar reads out where you are, not just how far in you are: it names the continent at world zoom, the region as you close in, then the majority terrain, then the very plot under your crosshair — nine bands, each with its own answer.

The Technology segment in the top bar is the research bar itself — it fills as the beakers land. Click it and the tech tree opens centred on whatever is being researched, where every tech is that same bar at a different value: full if it's known, filling if it's the current focus, an empty outline if it's still ahead.

This loading screen isn't only for show: the server ships a bill of materials for its baked world data, so the page totals the bytes and pulls the tech and building graphs while you read these — which is why the tech tree opens instantly instead of fetching a megabyte the moment you ask for it.

Notifications keep the simulation's clock, not yours: every event the sim logs lingers for thirty in-game days, reddening as its time runs out. Pause the world and a card hangs there mid-fade; run it at full speed and the same card is born, reddens and dies inside a couple of seconds. Right-click to be rid of one early.

A ruler colony collapses by design, but it does not simply stop: once its workforce falls below the floor, the survivors drain the banks, take to the road as a caravan, and the run ends there. The chronicle records which of the two endings it was — a colony that departed under its ruler, or one that simply ran out of people.

The Spectator Lobby is a room, not a menu: its chat belongs to no session at all, so you can talk there before you have picked anything to watch. Arrive mid-conversation and the last forty messages are replayed to you, then the rest arrive as they are said.

The Nations overlay flies real heraldry: all 1,527 Anbennar country flags are decoded from the mod's own TGA art and packed into a single WebP atlas, so the map can stamp each realm's flag and its proper localised name over its lands — and colour the whole ledger of nations — without a single extra download.

The tech tree unlocks units, not just buildings: each tech carries a second spectrum bar for the land units it grants, and its rail lists them grouped by caravan role — settler, worker, explorer, missionary, soldier — each naming its move points, its Caveman2Cosmos combat class, and the very skill that acting in that role would train.

Every figure in the top bar's colony strip is a doorway: click the population, the pool, the nobles — any of them — and the right rail unfolds the whole settlement, from its tax levers to a skill profile averaged across every household, down to a roster ranked with the ruler at its head. It is the same panel a wandering caravan opens when you click its icon on the map.

A session has no savegame file. What it has instead is its founding recipe — a seed, a scenario and a province — plus every order ever given to it, each stamped with the exact tick it took effect on. Replay the recipe, apply the orders in order, and the world reassembles itself down to the last household: the log is not a description of the run, it is the run.

Every household chooses its day's work: sell labor in town, or stay and work its own plot — raising first a bark hut, for no marriage is made under an open sky, then a workshop or two, and only then donating its hammers to the crown's building of the moment. A ruler with a seated player builds nothing unbidden: the world stops and awaits the decree.

Click a colony's city centre and the settlement opens: every plot it holds, the buildings standing on each, and the huts its households are hammering up right now — one progress bar per family. The crown's own queue sits beside them, and if the colony is yours you can reorder it, cancel it, or decree something new without waiting to be asked.

Zoom past a locale and the camera pitches over to 58 degrees and swings 45 degrees round — both numbers taken from Civ4 itself, whose CAMERA_LOWER_PITCH is 32 degrees above the horizon. The 45 is what stops you looking straight down the seams between the plots.

A mountain here is not a bump in the ground: the terrain stays nearly flat and Civ4's own peak model stands on the tile, exactly as the original does. Displacing the mesh instead made every peak boundary a cliff by construction.

Terrain is generated as a function of world position, not of province: a lattice of terrain patches is laid over the whole raster in absolute coordinates and each patch draws from a continuous climate field, so two neighbouring provinces agree exactly on their shared border — the map has no seams even though it is still generated one province at a time.

Anbennar's provinces are climate reference points, not climate cells. Each one paints its authored climate over its own pixels, and the map blurs the mosaic into a continuous temperature and humidity field — so a coastline warms into its hinterland instead of stepping.

The sand on a beach is real Civ4 paint, recovered by walking the alpha edge of the coast blend atlas and stepping inland — and it changes with latitude: pale and almost white in the tropics, golden in temperate seas, cold and grey near the poles.

The seabed is real terrain: every water plot carries a Civ4 terrain key — coast or open sea, in a polar, temperate or tropical palette, or freshwater lake — and tiles its own hand-painted ground texture under the shore, so a tropical shelf and a polar one are made of different art rather than different shades of the same blue.
